abstract.text: We analyze the effect of rising Chinese import competition between 1990 and 2007 on US local labor markets, exploiting cross-market variation in import exposure stemming from initial differences in industry specialization and instrumenting for US imports using changes in Chinese imports by other high-income countries. Rising imports cause higher unemployment, lower labor force participation, and reduced wages in local labor markets that house import-competing manufacturing industries. In our main specification, import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment. Transfer benefits payments for unemployment, disability, retirement, and healthcare also rise sharply in more trade-exposed labor markets. (JEL E24, F14, F16, J23, J31, L60, O47, R12, R23)

thesis.text: Rising Chinese import competition between 1990 and 2007 caused higher unemployment, lower labor-force participation, reduced wages, and higher transfer-benefit receipt in US local labor markets more exposed through initial manufacturing industry specialization.

One factor limiting trade’s impact on US labor is that historically, imports from low-wage countries have been small (Krugman 2000).

Though freer trade with countries at any income level may affect wages and employment, trade theory identifies low-wage countries as a likely source of disruption to high-wage labor markets (Krugman 2008).

source_span.start_text: I. Theoretical Motivation and Empirical Approach

sections.summary: Develops a monopolistic-competition trade model in which Chinese export-supply shocks reduce traded-sector labor demand in exposed US regions and, with trade imbalance, can reduce the size of the traded sector.

source_span.start_text: B. Empirical Approach

sections.summary: Defines import exposure per worker, instruments US imports from China with Chinese imports to eight other high-income countries, and discusses threats to identification.
sections.title: Empirical Approach and Instrumental Variables

source_span.start_text: II. Data Sources and Measurement

sections.summary: Describes UN Comtrade, County Business Patterns, Census/ACS data, commuting-zone mapping, and transfer-payment data.
sections.title: Data Sources and Measurement

source_span.start_text: III. The Impact of Trade Shocks on Manufacturing Employment

sections.summary: Presents the baseline 2SLS estimates showing that higher Chinese import exposure reduces manufacturing employment, and reports falsification tests using future exposure.
sections.title: Baseline Manufacturing Employment Effects

source_span.start_text: In Table 3, we augment the first difference model

source_span.start_text: B. Benchmarking the Impact of China Trade Exposure On US Manufacturing

sections.summary: Benchmarks the estimated decline against observed US manufacturing employment losses and compares China with low-income, Mexico/CAFTA, and other exporters.

source_span.start_text: IV. Beyond Manufacturing: Trade Shocks and Local Labor Markets

sections.summary: Shows weak population mobility, but sharp reallocation into unemployment and labor-force nonparticipation, especially among noncollege workers; links nonparticipation to SSDI take-up.
sections.title: Beyond Manufacturing: Population and Employment Status

source_span.start_text: B. Wage Effects

sections.summary: Finds negative average wage effects overall, with wages falling in nonmanufacturing but not significantly in manufacturing, suggesting local demand spillovers and composition effects.
sections.title: Wage Effects

source_span.start_text: V. Public Transfer Payments and Household Incomes

sections.summary: Shows that import exposure raises transfers, especially SSDI and medical benefits, with TAA playing a negligible role.

sections.summary: Tests alternative exposure measures: international third-market competition, intermediate inputs, net imports, gravity residuals, and factor content; results are broadly similar.
